Comprising 20 million relational statements, the COMET-ATOMIC knowledge graph successfully leverages the full symbolic representation of ATOMIC, enabling comprehensive coverage of complex knowledge relationships, such as causality, temporal sequencing, inference, and modality.  We demonstrate the utility of COMET-ATOMIC in three tasks: (1) identifying instances of complex knowledge relationships by utilizing the full relational coverage of COMET-ATOMIC, (2) detecting and interpreting modal verbs by annotating sentences with epistemic and alethic properties, and (3) constructing a graph-based language model that incorporates both symbolic and neural components by integrating COMET-ATOMIC with masked language and graph learning pretraining.

We have created a novel, versatile data processing pipeline, called Hi-GAL, designed specifically for handling the data collected by the Herschel Hi-GAL survey. The pipeline employs a combination of cutting-edge algorithms to efficiently manage a significant dataset of 1.2 TB, spanning 100 different Galactic regions. Its design is highly modular, allowing for the creation of 10 distinct nodes that can be easily adapted to produce ten distinct data products. These products range from basic to highly complex, including all-sky maps, spatial distribution plots, and catalogs of star-forming regions, each accompanied by diverse statistical and spatial analyses. The Hi-GAL pipeline's innovative architecture, incorporating both real-time and batch-based workflows, enables both online and offline data exploration. This allows users to seamlessly generate all 10 data products in under an hour using just 10 CPU cores, while still providing the computational power to process the entire dataset within a similar timeframe on larger systems. The Hi-GAL pipeline is now publicly available, providing a comprehensive resource for users to explore and analyze this dataset.

The unique metallicity spread observed within the first generation star population of NGC 2808 is well-documented, with a notable range of iron abundances. To further explore the origins of this phenomenon, we conducted a comprehensive study of elemental abundances in the cluster, focusing on a large sample of first generation stars. Using high-resolution, high-signal-to-noise ratio spectra, we determined the iron and several alpha element abundances. Our analysis revealed a substantial and unambiguous metallicity spread of 0.34, corroborating previous studies. Notably, this study is the first to conclusively confirm the metallicity spread in stars formed during the initial generation of the cluster.

A well-known phenomenon, Single File Motion, occurs when particles cannot bypass one another. Well-mixed fluids tend to follow this principle, and research has shown that entropy forces significantly impact collective behavior. However, the entropic forces' role in specific scenarios, such as first exit durations and collisions, remains unclear. To address this, we have derived an analytical model and used simulations to validate our findings. The results demonstrate that entropy forces substantially influence collisions and exit durations, and our model accurately predicts their entropic effects. Furthermore, we have shown that our model aligns with other theoretical predictions and can be applied to study collective exit durations as the system size increases.

Quantum mechanics' noncommutative operator property renders Bayes' rule inapplicable in the traditional sense. Through the development of a quantum probability framework utilizing the Stinespring dilation theorem, a new quantum version of Bayes' rule is derived, specifically addressing measurement outcomes in the Schrödinger picture projection postulate format. When applied to the von Neumann projector, this rule ensures consistency between inferred measurement results in distinct noncommutative quantum systems. Furthermore, an application of this rule to electron spin and linear optical systems demonstrates its feasibility.

The ultrarelativistic limit of energy density as influenced by quark number density, also known as the Equation of Condition (EOC), is examined for systems in the range of $1
\lesssim N_{\rm part}
\lesssim 100$ utilizing an advanced theoretical model that integrates quark dynamics and gluon behavior, and is valid across both confined and deconfined phases. 
Notably, this study reveals that the EOC is not entirely determined by the baryon number but also relies on temperature, indicating that EOC curves for different baryon densities cross each other.
Furthermore, our results show that EOC curves for systems with $N_{\rm part}
\lesssim 100$ are relatively uniform and, for temperatures above the phase transition point, are well-explained by an ideal gas model of quarks and gluons. 
This finding is significant for high-energy nuclear collisions and cosmic ray interactions, and is consistent with observed data on the average low-$p_{\rm T}$ multiplicity of produced particles in these processes.

In 1951, Milnor discovered a groundbreaking result, which stated that the cohomology groups of the Steenrod algebra over $\mathbb{F}_2$ possess an $\otimes$-decomposable structure. Following this discovery, he posed the question of whether this property holds true for fields other than $\mathbb{F}_2$. This article aims to provide a positive answer to Milnor's query, which states that the cohomology groups of the Steenrod algebra, $\H^{\ast}(\mathcal{A}_r, \mathbb{F}_2)$, possess non-trivial subrings, which are closed under the $\otimes$ operation, for any prime $p$.

Astronomical objects with circumstellar gas or protoplanetary disks can be studied in reflected Lyman-α ultraviolet light, but conventional near-UV optical instruments are hindered by Earth's atmosphere's strong emission and the object's continuum flux. We've developed a novel Lyman-alpha filter, featuring a multilayer dielectric structure, that effectively blocks visible and near-IR wavelengths and sharpens the passband to 5.8 Angstroms, maintaining high quantum efficiency of the underlying detector. This prototype filter has demonstrated an impressive 8 orders of magnitude of optical density and transmits approximately 40% of the Lyman-alpha wavelength. We've also observed the filter's resilience under intense illumination, high-speed electron bombardment, and gamma-ray exposure, showcasing its potential for detecting faint Lyman-α signals on near-Earth instruments.

This research investigates the problem of managing complex network systems efficiently and sustainably in real-time using graph filter techniques. The research focuses on systems exhibiting symmetry, as they arise in various real-world applications. The research aims to develop a method for optimizing dynamic graph filters on large networks while accounting for potential disruptions and changes. The proposed solution, inspired by ideas from distributed control, leverages graph filters to minimize system performance losses. The research demonstrates that its approach can be efficiently implemented as a graph filter, resulting in computational and communication complexities comparable to existing methods. The proposed distributed solution offers a lower communication cost and higher scalability compared to existing methods. The research validates its efficacy through numerical simulations.

A visual search system's image database is constantly evolving and expanding, which makes it difficult to efficiently manage and minimize computation.
A novel, memory-efficient method for handling dynamic visual indexing is presented, utilizing a hardware-accelerated GPU for speed and optimization.
Our strategy involves leveraging lightweight hashing and then converting good pairs for more accurate retrieval through the use of Siamese neural networks.
To tackle the challenge of incremental growth, our system employs a hierarchical vector quantization and sparse indexing scheme that maintains low memory consumption and allows for the efficient addition of new data.
A single GPU can now efficiently process and manage a dataset consisting of hundreds of millions of images, while supporting real-time retrieval and continuous expansion.

This paper introduces a secure communication method over noisy channels that relies on physical randomness rather than shared secret keys. Our proposed scheme utilizes the inherent properties of narrowband wideband noise to generate random patterns that can be used for authentication. To account for noise variability, we've developed an adaptive error-correcting code that can accurately verify transmitted messages. To optimize verification performance, we've designed specific channel models and error-correcting codes tailored to our purpose. Experimental results demonstrate the scheme's effectiveness, with near-zero verification error rates, and analysis of computational complexity shows it to be suitable for real-world applications.

A previous study on an integrable model, which described a particle moving in a dispersionless potentials landscape, was published by A. V. Zaburdaev in 2009. The quantum version of this model was found to maintain its integration properties in the work of D. Bessis and G. M. Zuhayti from 2009. The current research delves into the connection between the quantum model and the classical model in the context of washboard potentials. The quantum model's spectrum is calculated and compared to the dispersionless potentials, which were found to be quantum for specific washboard potentials. The WKB method is used to derive the energy levels of these potentials in both the deep and shallow potential limits. The findings are then applied to a quark-antiquark system in a string theory, which is relevant to both deep and shallow potentials. The research also provides a new, simpler way to find the weak coupling energy levels of the system.

This research introduces a novel, non-parametric method for estimating impulse reaction curves in time series data, where the influence of shocks is localized in time, yet interconnected across various equations. Our approach combines the flexibility of Frydman and Yang's (2017) flexible local projection technique with a stochastic regression model feature, enabling precise parameter constraints in each time step while maintaining the method's overall adaptability. We validate our method's performance through extensive simulation studies and apply it to two real-world scenarios: assessing the economic impact of central bank policy reactions and analyzing the effect of one-sector shock on economic growth patterns under different financial conditions.

A charge moving in a magnetic field is referred to as a Landau charge, and the researchers explore the behavior of the charge's field from the perspective of QED. They discover that the charge generates anisotropic fluctuations in the electromagnetic field, resulting in a torque that causes a vacuum to be V-shapedly polarized around the charge. The density of this polarization peaks at a certain distance from the charge and is oriented perpendicular to both the charge's momentum and the magnetic field. The researchers also investigate two scenarios: when the charge is at rest and when it moves slowly. They find that the anisotropic vacuum energy remains unchanged under Lorentz transformations in these scenarios. Moreover, they predict that this phenomenon can be observed in the vacuum created by electrons in a magnetic field, and suggest that it may be detectable through the disruption of the symmetry of a 2D electron gas by a nearby impurity.

The Task of Fine-Grained Network Entity Recognition (FGNET) is an essential component of Natural Language Processing (NLP) and requires distinguishing sub-categories of entities within a predefined framework. Traditional methods for FGNET, which focus on improving representation quality or enhancing interaction among entities, often neglect to consider the inherent hierarchical structure of the task. To address this limitation, a novel network design, FGNET-RH, is proposed for FGNET, leveraging refinement within a hyperbolic space to capture the hierarchical relationships among entities. FGNET-RH incorporates two modules: a local entity refinement module that leverages adjacent words to enhance entity representation, and a global entity refinement module that utilizes the entire context to facilitate interaction among adjacent words and entire sentences. Extensive experiments conducted on four benchmark datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of FGNET-RH, outperforming existing models and highlighting its superiority in FGNET applications.

This paper provides proofs for upper bounds on the Hankel determinants of the second order for functions within the univalent class $\mathcal{S}$ and a more generalized class, specifically those with negative coefficients. We establish that the class $\mathcal{S}$ has specific bounds for these determinants and provide sufficient conditions for the preservation of univalence under these conditions.

Achieving optimal resource utilization and energy efficiency in cloud data centers is a pressing issue. Excessively allocated resources lead to increased operational costs and unnecessary energy consumption, whereas underutilized servers should have their resources reassigned. Load distribution techniques aim to balance resources across multiple VMs, but they are typically triggered by a VM's termination, causing delays in achieving optimal load distribution. To address this issue, we introduce Prepartition, a novel virtual machine reservation strategy. It facilitates load distribution by coordinating the resource allocation process before the relevant VMs are started, eliminating the need to wait for a VM to terminate. We evaluate Prepartition against two traditional approaches using various metrics, including the number of VMs required, achieved load distribution, and execution time. Our results demonstrate that Prepartition achieves better load distribution with comparable number of VMs and similar time efficiency.

In many economic settings, outcomes are determined by the strategic interactions of multiple agents, often resulting in a Nash equilibrium. However, individual agents may not always behave optimally in response to one another, a phenomenon that can be observed when reactions lag behind each other. This phenomenon necessitates forecasting future reactions based on past actions, a complex task. This study introduces the first neural architecture specifically designed to tackle this challenge, a Fixed Point Network (FPN). FPNs iteratively converge to a predicted equilibrium and demonstrate superior performance in a range of economic scenarios, surpassing the FNN baseline approach in various forecasting tasks.

This research investigates the dimensionless causal influence, a metric quantifying the effect of a variable on another within a given acyclic causal network. A newly derived upper limit for this causal influence is presented in terms of the variables' standardized normal distributions and the absolute value of their conditional mutual information, providing a significant improvement over previous bound estimations. The practical utility of this new bound is demonstrated through its application to the calculation of the maximum causal influence in high-dimensional data, specifically within the context of the Ising model, where an explicit analytical expression is developed. The research also establishes a direct relationship between the maximum causal influence and the largest eigenvector associated with a specific adjacency matrix eigenvalue, facilitating efficient computational approaches for estimating this metric in complex data sets.

A previously proposed stealth attack on Linear Time-Invariant (LTI) systems, known as the Signal Attack, has been proven to remain undetected by residual generators while causing observable effects on system outputs. This discovery led to the development of a countermeasure involving a specific detector. However, due to limitations in adjusting its parameters, this detector often suffers from false alarms. In response, we introduce a cross-checking approach that leverages predictive outputs to create a structure-compatible monitor, which effectively identifies signal attacks. By integrating remaining system components into the detection mechanism, this monitor can be finely tuned to minimize false alarms. A thorough analysis of both monitors is provided, accompanied by a proof of its compatibility with the original structure and examples demonstrating its superior performance compared to existing methods.

This paper presents research on short text summarization across multiple languages, with a particular focus on Indian languages. A new, unsupervised graph-based summarization model called GAE-ISumm has been developed to address the challenges associated with Indian languages, including low resource availability and complex grammar. The model demonstrates improved performance over existing graph-based and other language models, with an average ROUGE score increase of 6.1 points on ISumm, 8.1 points on HindiSum, and 4.1 points on MarathiSum datasets. The results of this research are available, including the code and pre-trained models, for further study and replication.

A s-ring is defined as a set with two operations, * and +, where is a set with these operations. We investigate s-rings that match the dimensions of a finite ring R in specific cases, including when R has no invertible elements or has no nilpotent elements of degree three or higher, which reveal that these s-ring types are essentially finite rings themselves.

The five visual binary systems, which include the accelerating stars HD 127474, HD 147513, HD 152205, and HD 154443, have been studied in detail.  By utilizing Gaia EDR3 data, we determined the current positions, velocities, and distances of these systems.  We found that HD 147513, which was previously categorized as a single star, is actually a wide binary system with an orbital period of 1.1 million years.  By analyzing the motion of HD 147513, we were able to constrain the mass of its unseen companion to 0.1-0.2 solar masses.  We also determined the distances to the other four binary systems, which were previously uncertain, and calculated their masses based on their motions.  We found that HD 127474, which was previously thought to have a mass of 1.02-1.08 solar masses, actually has an additional unseen companion with a mass of 0.07-0.13 solar masses.  We also determined the distances to the other binary systems, which were previously estimated to be 1.2-1.8 kpc, and calculated their masses based on their motions.  We found that HD 152205, which was previously thought to have a mass

Variational Autoencoders (VAEs) are widely used in unsupervised learning, combining an encoder-decoder architecture with a variational regularization term. The traditional VAE approach, however, typically assumes a likelihood based on data likelihood, which may not always be suitable. This work explores a regularized variational autoencoder framework centered on a least-squares likelihood, particularly suited for regression tasks. The proposed model incorporates an additional regularization term to control the complexity of the encoder architecture, which is often overlooked in standard VAEs. The theoretical analysis demonstrates that minimum change in data likelihood and minimum changes in encoder architecture objectives are interconnected and yield similar optimal solutions. The empirical evaluation of this model shows that it achieves improved performance compared to existing models that incorporate regularization, which in turn outperform unregularized models.

A blockchain is a distributed ledger technology that maintains records across multiple nodes within a network. These records, known as blocks, are secured and verified using cryptographic methods and a consensus mechanism that ensures integrity and reliability within the blockchain ecosystem. By linking events chronologically and securing them through encryption, a blockchain provides an unalterable and verifiable record of data entries within a network, making it ideal for secure data storage and tamper-proof record-keeping. This paper presents a novel approach to integrating a blockchain with a smart home monitoring system that leverages the GPS location of IoT devices to enhance the efficiency of block verification and reduce energy consumption of the IoT network, enabling efficient scalability of the system.

A recent deep learning-based method has been developed for quantifying continuous signal components, known as L-variables, in the context of wireless communication. This approach leverages neural networks to achieve high-quality quantization, thereby increasing the spectral efficiency of wireless systems. In this paper, a novel deep learning architecture is presented, incorporating a convolutional layer, which significantly reduces the computational complexity of this efficiency-enhancing quantization process. By substituting the complex traditional quantization layer with the lower complexity convolutional layer, the method achieves substantial reductions in computational requirements. Furthermore, it is demonstrated that the method outperforms its predecessors in terms of both channel performance and transmission distance capabilities.

For a planar graph, we can visualize it by having a specific root node positioned at the top, with all its connected edges directed away from the root, as opposed to being directed towards the root, as in traditional methods. This concept, which was explored by J. Bang-Jensen et al., involves single-rooted acyclic graphs, a topic that was later adapted to the study of planarity in parameterized complexity. Researchers investigated the complexity of various single-rooted graph problems, such as planarity and specific subgraph patterns, as well as the complexity of drawing a given directed graph without intersections, based on various size constraints. A key outcome of their study was the development of an algorithm with a runtime of O(n^2) for checking the planarity of a graph, and O(n^2) for converting a planar graph into a valid drawing, which was further extended to account for single-rooted graphs in linear time. Building on this, the team established a polynomial algorithm for drawing a graph with single-rooted edges, as well as investigating single-rooted graph subgraph patterns, specifically path and tree patterns, as well as the complexity of the general problem of drawing a graph without intersections, based on various size constraints.

Crowdsourcing projects often produce large datasets, but they're often plagued by uncertainty due to inconsistencies in quality. This research explores a unique approach to mitigate the effects of uncertainty in these large-scale crowdsourced datasets by employing an ensemble modeling strategy. The proposed approach integrates a human-softmax distribution and an entropic uncertainty metric to enhance the reliability of annotated datasets. The 'human-softmax' distribution, a quality control measure, aggregates the output of multiple models, while the entropic metric quantifies uncertainty in label quality. The ensemble modeling strategy, which combines numerous models, is designed to address uncertainty in crowdsourced datasets. The paper showcases the efficacy of this approach through its successful application on the Amazon Mechanical Turk dataset.

We demonstrate that for certain given semiflows, the computation of finite-time Lyapunov vectors and matrices can be accurately performed by analyzing transfer operators associated with specific semigroups. Notably, the norm of these transfer operators exhibits a decreasing trend as time progresses, with this tendency providing an assessment of the complexity in computing aforementioned quantities for any given time frame.

A recent paper provided exact constructions and bounds for the size of covering arrays with strength 2 over various levels. This work aims to improve upon these results by reducing the size of the covering arrays through a series of novel methods. Specifically, a new method is utilized to generate covering arrays from the product of two smaller arrays. Additionally, a specific construction is utilized for level-2 arrays and a generalization of the Pierce method is employed to produce covering arrays of size strength 2 from the product of two smaller arrays. This work also introduces a specific covering array graph concept which enables the production of smaller covering arrays through the use of graph products. Ultimately, these methods are utilized to create covering arrays that outperform the previous best results in numerous cases.

This paper demonstrates that determining the optimal winning probability for nonlocal games played using the most closely correlated states has become solvable through an exact method known as semidefinite programming. To achieve this, we show that any payoff function associated with such games can be expressed as a semidefinite program. Furthermore, this development is expanded to encompass noisy correlations between multiple particles. This study builds on the principles of quantum entanglement, which was first utilized by Bell to illustrate the distinction between quantum and classical physics, and has since been applied in various fields, including data transmission, storage, and computation. Notably, this research utilizes semidefinite programming, a technique originating from optimization theory, to study quantum systems.

A paper by Alrawi et al. presented a novel method for automatically reproducing software bugs, known as PathFinder, which is based on a genetic algorithm. Their approach was found to be more successful than a random search method, with PathFinder locating a valid input sequence in approximately 96% of cases where sequences of inputs with up to 1000 steps were known to cause the software to fail. In cases where a random search was unsuccessful, PathFinder required only about 20% of the effort. While PathFinder was successful in identifying sequences that triggered the software error, these sequences did not always accurately represent the original cause of the bug.

Theoretical models suggest a connection between two types of vortex grids, a 4-square and a square, within the phase diagram of cuprate superconductors. To explore this hypothesis, we analyzed small-bias conductance in thin YBCO crystals using magnetic force microscopy and microwave radiation. Our study revealed that the transition between these vortex grids occurs at significantly lower magnetic fields than previously estimated, approximately 10 times the Hains field. Additionally, the theoretical framework that predicts this transition indicates that the Hains field should depend on the crystal's thickness, an assertion that we also confirmed through microwave measurements on the same YBCOs.

Researchers investigated thermal photon emission in nucleus-nucleus collisions using the JAM model, which simulates quark-gluon plasma's mechanical properties through its internal parameters, $\eta$ (viscosity-to-entropy density ratio) and $T_0$ (onset temperature). They analyzed the anisotropic flow ($v_2$) of photons in central Au+Au collisions at various energies, from E$_{cm}$ = 7.7 GeV to 53.6 GeV, and found that lower $\eta$ or $T_0$ values in JAM lead to increased $\int E d\sigma/dEd$ for $E < 4$ GeV. Crucially, they discovered that different $\eta$ or $T_0$ combinations yield distinct $\langle v_2 \rangle$ values, allowing for unique determination of QCD hadronization parameters based on data. This also implies that JAM can be effectively "tuned" to accurately model the actual properties of the system.

Researchers have been using theoretical and computational methods to investigate the magnetic properties that naturally arise in materials with triangular structures, focusing on both knee-length and kite-shaped (kagome) lattice patterns. Numerous studies have found that certain types of short-range magnetic orders, such as the 6, 12_2, 21_3 states and 5, 12_3, 21_5 states, are commonly observed in the kagome lattice pattern. Interestingly, the 6, 12_2, 21_3 state has also been identified as a common short-range magnetic pattern in the triangular lattice pattern, further suggesting that these two types of magnetic patterns are closely related.

This paper addresses a fundamental issue in large-scale field and social science experiments involving multiple treatments, where researchers often lack the ability to conduct fully randomized trials due to resource limitations and constraints. As a result, multiple treatments are often paired with various control groups, resulting in multiple comparison datasets. Under these conditions, traditional FDR controlling procedures may fail, particularly when dealing with dependent datasets, which can severely distort p-value distributions. To overcome this challenge, we propose the Treatment Effect Identification with Controlled FDR under Dependence (T-EFID) procedure, designed to accurately estimate and control p-value dependence. By leveraging control groups, T-EFID achieves exact control over the FDR under controlled conditions, demonstrating superior performance in simulations and real-world applications.

Consider a point particle moving at constant speed $v$ in an expanding universe with radius $R$, subject to a linear frictional force proportional to the particle's momentum and the rate of change of $R$. The frictional influence causes the particle's velocity to gradually decrease, eventually reaching zero. Our objective is to derive an expression that relates the time $t$ required for this deceleration to the universe's scale factor and its rate of change.

The long-standing anomalies of the muon's magnetic dipole moment and the W boson mass are resolved through the type-X Two Higgs Doublet Model, specifically by introducing charged Higgs particles. This model, which aligns with Higgs alignment and the vacuum stability, indicates that the mass of a scalar Higgs is greater than 240 GeV, as well as requiring a negative $\tan\beta$ in the range of 3-10. Furthermore, in scenarios where $|\tan\beta|>1$, the mass of the charged Higgs exceeds $350$ GeV.

The increasing adoption of automated code entry through Natural Language Processing has brought about new challenges in locating code concepts. Quicker identification of concepts is crucial for maintaining developer productivity, but this is hindered by two key issues: the need for developers to recall and articulate the code concept in natural language, and variation in how code concepts are described. These challenges are exacerbated by the rapid evolution of code concepts, which can render traditional search ineffective. To address these issues, we propose QUICKAR, an advanced concept-finding system that utilizes crowd-sourced knowledge to facilitate code concept location through automatic instruction generation. By leveraging a crowd-sourced platform, QUICKAR streamlines the process by which developers can leverage collective knowledge to identify code concepts more efficiently.

The phenomenon of entrainment, where speakers subtly adjust their utterances to mirror each other, is a well-documented aspect of conversational speech. This adaptive process, crucial for maintaining a cohesive dialogue, has been the subject of numerous studies employing both traditional and modern machine learning techniques. The paper presents the first known application of unsupervised deep learning to identify and measure the linguistic features that contribute to the most synchronized conversations. The proposed method, which involves feature extraction from pre-trained neural networks, is complemented by the development of a new metric for the unsupervised detection of intonation entrainment. The experiments conducted demonstrate the superiority of the developed metric in the accurate and efficient identification of entrainment instances.

A recent version of the CSED web resource has been released, providing a comprehensive suite of open-source tools for the visual analysis of SNe Ia light curves, spectra, and data representations. The resource incorporates traditional methods for SNe Ia imaging and spectrophotometry, alongside novel techniques utilizing machine learning-based representation of spectral data through deep convolutional neural networks. The resource has been extensively tested with both simulated and actual supernovae data, encompassing contributions from the RCSE project and other collaborators.

Temporal action segmentation is a complex task that requires accurately identifying the timing of actions within videos. One effective approach, known as Self-supervised Action segmentation, leverages self-supervision to learn representations directly from videos without the need for labeled data. One such method, SS-CAP, utilizes self-supervised learning with Color and Flow features, which have shown promising results. However, these features are limited and may not capture the full complexity of actions. Our proposed solution, SSCAP, extends this approach by introducing a Self-supervised Co-occurrence Action framework that combines color, flow, and action information from video data. By training SSCAP in a self-supervised manner, it can learn richer and more effective representations that lead to improved performance. Our experiments demonstrate that SSCAP achieves state-of-the-art results on benchmark datasets THUMOS14 and Kinetics, surpassing SSCAP and other supervised methods.

Aa the beginning of this research, we apply current algebra to investigate pentaquark states, with a specific emphasis on those with hidden charm. These states are analyzed in terms of their mass, coupling, and decay ratios. The results confirm the existence of two distinct types of pentaquark states, with different characteristics and decay properties. The findings also show that the p5876 resonance observed by LHCb can be described within this analysis, and predict additional resonances for further experimental investigation. The research highlights the unique features of the pentaquark states and their decays, with a specific emphasis on their mass differences, decay ratios, and production mechanisms. The analysis of the pentaquark states reveals a rich and complex structure, with specific properties that distinguish them from other hadronic states. The results provide a specific framework for understanding the pentaquark states and their decays, with specific predictions for their production and decay rates.

In computer science education, particularly in software engineering, a crucial aspect of learning is understanding the importance of high-quality feedback in improving student performance. While there's a growing consensus that inquiry-based learning methods are more effective than traditional instruction, there's a lack of empirical evidence to support this claim, especially in the context of software engineering. A recent study aimed to fill this knowledge gap by investigating the effectiveness of an enhanced inquiry-based approach, specifically in the area of software testing. Employing a within-subject experimental design, the researchers compared the effectiveness of three different feedback mechanisms: enhanced inquiry-based, traditional thorough, and basic thorough. A survey of 120 software engineering students revealed that an enhanced inquiry-based approach resulted in the highest quality of software testing, outperforming both traditional and thorough methods.

In semi-supervised domain adaptation, a common challenge arises when models trained on source domains experience significant degradation when applied to tasks with abundant labeled data, due to the lack of diverse datasets for thorough evaluation. This phenomenon, known as hypothesis shift, is a critical consideration in domain adaptation research. To address this issue, a proposed approach aims to mitigate hypothesis shift in domain adaptation without access to a representative dataset. A semi-supervised cross-memorization method is introduced to counter the overfitting of deep neural networks by storing and referencing key features from the source domain. A diversification-based selection technique is also developed to ensure the robustness of these methods across various datasets. Experimental results demonstrate the efficacy of these innovations in adapting models to datasets facing the hypothesis shift problem, with substantial improvements observed across different scenarios.

The primary objectives of the deep space exploration missions are limited by the vast distances that need to be covered. To overcome these limitations, advanced propulsion systems are needed, which include chemical, nuclear, and possibly other innovative technologies. This research focuses on gas-core engine designs, specifically those incorporating a liquid fuel and oxidizer core, which undergo combustion within a magnetic or permeable containment field, causing the core to rotate at high speeds and expel plasma for thrust generation. The results of numerical simulations for various engine configurations are presented, and several key findings are discussed, including the existence of multiple steady-state solutions and the variation of the core's shape with the applied magnetic field.

Designing optimal neural networks to analyze vast data from astroparticle detectors is crucial for determining the origin of incoming particles within the detector volume or from outside it, avoiding misinterpretations due to muon interactions. We utilize the deep neural network framework to examine various optimal classification strategies, weighing features that accurately distinguish external from internal events. We assess the performance of the domain-informed neural network approach and find it significantly outperforms the standard method, with classification accuracy reaching 99.5% after analyzing 10 million events in the HAWC-HERA prototype.

The number of characterized exoplanet atmospheres is growing, particularly those with large, gas-giant atmospheres exhibiting distinct spectral features. As research into these atmospheres advances, the need for comprehensive, customized spectral cross-sections becomes increasingly important. In response to this need, the EXOplenet INdex (EXOPLINES) has been established, providing a comprehensive database of molecular absorption cross-sections for 18 key molecules and their isotopes, covering 160-6000 nm wavelength ranges. The EXOPLINES database is tailored to the atmospheric conditions of gas-exhibiting exoplanets, particularly those situated in the sub-Neptune to giant-exoplanet mass range, with atmospheric temperatures spanning from 100 to 3000 K. The line lists were carefully analyzed and adjusted to accommodate potential systematic errors, ultimately allowing for the creation of custom absorption cross-sections for use in transmission, emission, and thermal equilibrium spectra of exoplanetary atmospheres.

This paper proposes novel principles to enhance the explanation of the grounding process in Answer Set Programming. These principles aim to provide a more structured understanding of the grounding process by breaking it down into distinct stages guided by specific rules. We acknowledge the inherent complexity of the grounding process and note that any single high-level abstraction will necessarily be a partial representation. To address this, we introduce two complementary strategies for structuring the grounding process: one decomposes it into sequential steps defined by specific criteria, while the other views grounding as a series of refinements to the program's syntax. The introduced abstractions are designed to capture the general flow of the grounding process, incorporating details that may be program-specific or specific to the grounder used.

In the field of quantum resource theories, we have developed a novel method to measure the quantum advantage, which applies to any chosen resource definition. This method relies on a specific entanglement assumption made at the start of a task. We demonstrate that this quantum advantage can be expressed as the ratio between two costs: the complexity of a certain quantum circuit, which transforms a random input into a desired resource state, divided by the circuit's complexity that achieves the same outcome without any entanglement. Our results show that this method is equivalent to a standard measure of entanglement when no initial entanglement is present. In scenarios with some entanglement, our method provides an upper limit of the required communication between parties. By examining these ideas through various examples, we see that this method is versatile and can provide precise results for a wide range of situations.

This paper explores the potential of learning probability distributions from the first two moments, highlighting its theoretical and practical applications. We examine and discuss the underlying principles behind this problem, including the underlying geometry and the relationships between different distributions, as well as the key theorems and open questions. Our analysis also considers the broader implications of this problem and the feasibility of using the first two moments to capture a distribution's essential characteristics. Additionally, we discuss the main approaches to solving this problem and the limitations of these methods. Our work aims to provide a comprehensive overview of the current state of the field and to identify future research directions.

We develop a novel class of multivariate time series models featuring non-fixed marginal distributions, derived from the Poisson process. An extension of the GARCH model is proposed, enabling inference of parameters in large samples through maximum likelihood estimation. Additionally, we establish asymptotic properties such as consistency and efficiency under specific tail behavior constraints. Empirical results show that our approach effectively handles data sets with non-stationary marginal behavior and heavy tails better than models assuming fixed marginal distributions.

A recent breakthrough has shown the existence of LDPC quantum codes that can effectively combat random row and column errors. Interestingly, there are instances of these codes where the original models result in exponential decoding times, but our work demonstrates codes that can efficiently decode linearly. Specifically, we have developed a new class of good quantum LDPC codes with a constant number of checks, featuring a large relative distance. These codes can be decoded using a relatively small number of parallel parallel runs of a suboptimal classical decoder, resulting in a linear time decoding process. This new code construction has significant implications for the quantum capacity of LDPC channels, providing a specific example of this capacity with a defined relative quantum entropy.

The Distributed Complexity of Graph Dominating Sets is a widely studied problem within the model of distributed computing, particularly within the $T\mathcal{C}$ and $\mathcal{C\mathcal{O}}$ frameworks. Research has primarily focused on characterizing problems solvable within these models, with significant breakthroughs achieved through reductions and upper bounds on the dependency of the running time on the graph parameters. Specifically, upper bounds on the dependency of the running time on the radius of the graph have been established for Minimum Dominating Set in unweighted graphs, as well as for several problems in weighted graphs. A key limitation of these results is that their dependency on the radius is superlinear, whereas linear dependency is optimal. This paper seeks to address this limitation by establishing a linear dependency on the radius of $O(n)$ for Minimum Dominating Set, specifically for sparse high-girth graphs within the $T\mathcal{C}$ model. Achieving this result, we rely on the sparsity of the graph, which enables us to obtain a dominating set of size $O(n)$ on sparse graphs of high girth through the use of a Maximum Independent Set, leveraging the aforementioned upper bound. Moreover, our result is further strengthened by showing that, for sparse graphs of high girth, we can obtain a dominating set of size $O(n)$ within the $\mathcal{C\mathcal{O}}$ model, in which nodes are anonymous, and the degree of each node

A theoretical model has been developed to study a three-dimensional disordered topological insulator with corner states that emerge from a unique topological property known as bulk-surface correspondence. In this model, corner states are found to decouple from the surface states when a specific type of topological order is considered, which is characterized by a non-zero Chern-Simons term. The corner states exhibit a power-law localization that results from a topological term in the effective field theory, and this behavior is confirmed through numerical calculations that reveal a change in the critical exponent for the correlation length as a result of a higher-order topological insulator correction.

Recent searches for supersymmetry at the CMS experiment have primarily focused on hadronic final states, employing zero-lepton and four-lepton triggers. Data collected from 2016 with 35.9 inverse femtobarns of data at 13 TeV have been analyzed in conjunction with various supersymmetry searches. Four searches were combined to enhance sensitivity: searches involving mono- and dilepton final states paired with general zeros, as well as trilepton final states paired with top quarks. A combined analysis of these combinations has been conducted to enhance sensitivity to supersymmetric particle production. Furthermore, the CMS collaboration has recently released searches utilizing international datasets, collected by the ATLAS and CMS experiments with integrated luminosity of up to 139 inverse femtobarns. This presentation will provide an update on the latest results from the CMS collaboration, specifically focusing on deepening supersymmetry parameter space exploration and expanding into new regions of the parameter space.

A pioneering approach in computer graphics, radiance caching, efficiently resolves global illumination by storing and utilizing radiance values. This method's limitations in achieving high resolution restrict its use in applications requiring detailed visuals. Our work introduces the first effective integration of neural rendering with radiance caching, enabling efficient storage of illumination values at arbitrary target points. Our novel neural radiance cache system combines traditional ray tracing, high-quality surface rendering, and neural rendering techniques to optimize storage efficiency and enable scalable brightness increases. Our method also includes techniques to mitigate color bleeding, enhance value reliability, and support multi-scale ray tracing. Through comprehensive evaluations, our neural radiance cache significantly outperforms multi-scale path tracing, while allowing for granular control of image quality, particularly beneficial in rendering pipelines such as radiance tracing.

This study presents the initial results from the first year of the SOAR Interferometric Campaign, which took place in 2021. The 3.5-meter SOAR telescope, located in Chile, was paired with the MIRA beam combiner to connect two separate 3-m mirrors in two observing stations in La Silla. During the year-long campaign, 16 hours of binary star observations were collected, yielding 14 successful datasets. The observed stars span a wide range of separation distances, from 0.14 to 1.1 arcseconds, and the study provides the most precise measurements of their angular distances. Furthermore, the data collected enables the determination of key variables, such as orbital periods, eccentricities, and mass ratios, as well as the study of long-term changes in projected separation and orbital phase. The observed mass ratios are in good agreement with those obtained through photometric methods, and the study highlights the potential of interferometric techniques to uncover previously unknown features in binary stars, such as circumstellar disks and circumstellar disks around binary systems.

We investigate the relationship between celestial chiral algebras and two other areas: the chiral algebras developed by Bezrukikhin et al. in 2018 and a newly identified duality known as hue-kinematics, first proposed by Chen and Roest in 2021. It is demonstrated that the BCC celestial algebra is a more comprehensive version of the SU(2) hue theory. As an application of the hue-kinematics duality, the BCC theory is found to be integrable, with the ability to construct an infinite set of conserved charges that respect their respective equations of motion and collision processes.

A solar jet, specifically the one with the number 20191117T08, was observed using the distributed LOFAR telescope, which provided high-frequency data of the solar corona. The imaging results revealed a complex jet structure along with a distinct piston-driven shock wave, along with a brighter region at the leading edge. Spectral analysis showed an electron temperature of 1.5 million Kelvin and a 10 billion electron Volts of non-thermal energy within the shock region. The coexistence of shock-driven and jet-driven components was found to be unique. The research revealed that the piston-driven shock produced significant energy release, with energy release rates of 10^10 to 10^12 erg per second, which is comparable to the energy released by flares.

A generalized model of two Higgs doublets, known as the GFZ2DM and incorporating a $U(1)_{FZ}$ symmetry, is analyzed in relation to experimental anomalies observed in B-meson decays and the muon's anomalous magnetic moment. Our analysis, based on an all-encompassing likelihood assessment, reveals that the GFZ2DM's 2H2E and 2H2µ solutions are the most viable in explanation of the B-meson decay anomalies, while only the latter presents a potential solution to the muon's anomalous magnetic moment when considering current constraints. Our results, in line with previous findings, indicate that GFZ2DM's explanation of the anomalies is highly dependent on specific flavour textures and that any viable explanation necessitates breaking of lepton flavour universality in 2-fermion annihilation processes. Furthermore, our findings show that, in general, GFZ2DM's fit to the flavour anomalies and the muon's anomalous magnetic moment is highly incompatible with current precision electroweak data and direct Higgs searches.

This study proposes a new framework for randomly evolving vortex paths, represented as functional stochastic differential equations. We examine the consistency between the vortex dynamics model, in terms of path measures, with a given 2D fluid fluid described by a fluid variance. We investigate the existence and feasibility of functional stochastic differential equations and establish a connection between these equations and 2D fluid models under the framework of weak solutions. The study further includes several instances of 2D fluid scenarios where the existence and feasibility of the corresponding functional stochastic differential equations can be demonstrated, including cases of both smooth and singular initial conditions.

The calculation of reduced density matrices and entanglement measures for specific optical network configurations has been carried out using Gaussian states, yielding measurable results for intermode von Neumann entanglement, Theil's noise, and the logarithmic negativity. These metrics exhibit significant correlations with the complexity of the task in linear and quadratic boson sampling, revealing notable advantages for Theil's noise in distinguishing tasks of greater difficulty.

In temporal analysis, researchers often tackle the classification problem of sequences, but these sequences are typically long and limited in their descriptive power. To address this, a novel approach has been developed, allowing for the effective handling of short sequences with many dimensions. This approach is demonstrated in temporal analysis across various medical fields, such as analyzing cell division and the behavior of individual cells, where researchers examine complex biological processes. To demonstrate its effectiveness, a guided approach is utilized to design a customized neural network architecture, allowing for accurate classification even with the limited amount of data available in such medical studies. This approach also showcases its versatility by applying it to both classification and clustering tasks.

A recurrent neural network, particularly a simple variant with one hidden unit and symmetric connections, is analyzed for its performance in the Bernoulli process Ber[ρ], where it must predict the output of a stochastic process given previous observations. It is found that such a network, even with infinite length input, can only effectively utilize a finite history of nine steps or less. Furthermore, it is demonstrated that the network is capable of representing its understanding of the Bernoulli process, similar to a belief in a specific range, based on its final hidden state. The model that the network develops is an updated estimate of the Bernoulli process's parameter ρ, similar to a belief. Building on these findings, it is suggested that the presence of a hidden unit in such a network indicates its intrinsic time horizon for making predictions and its method of integrating new information to revise its understanding of a stochastically varying environment.

Deep learning-based models have achieved top results in video action detection, but they often struggle when there's only minimal labeling due to their reliance on pre-trained image features that overlook spatial context. To address this, we propose a novel graph-based model that leverages attention mechanisms to capture action-related regions and a graph convolutional network that utilizes local and global dependencies in video data. Through the use of instance-wise attention, our model identifies critical spatial areas and generates meaningful action representations, while a graph convolutional network refines these with a data-driven approach. With this, our method surpasses current state-of-the-art models on THM1K and Kinetics datasets, even when trained using only context weak labels.

The 2021 Image Similarity Challenge (2021-ISC) focused on the metric learning and image retrieval tasks, building on previous years with the challenge's second installment. A total of 47 teams participated, submitting 102 entries to the public track. Three new datasets were introduced: the 'Sentinel-2' satellite dataset, 'AG News' textual dataset, and the 'MIMIC-CT' medical dataset. In the public track, the top three teams were ranked as follows: first, the "On the Verge of Precision" team with the R@1 metric score of 64.3; second, "Aristotle" with 63.9; and third, "A New Hope" with 63.4. Notably, the challenge's organizers created the BINARY track, which restricted entries to binary embeddings, and saw the "Monash University" team take the top spot, along with "Aristotle" and "The Next" in fourth and fifth overall. Post-challenge, participants and organizers collaborated on the OpenIR platform, which hosts the post-challenge leaderboard, dataset tools, and analysis tools. The paper presents a comprehensive summary of challenges, datasets, results, and findings, including an analysis of the results and an exploration of the most effective approaches and their potential applications.

This work explores the long-term behavior of a type of stochastic process that undergoes transformation and degradation over a confined area, along with a closely related mathematical model. Although mathematical models of stochastic processes are often considered stable over long periods, this specific type tends to become unstable when incorporating certain conditions that simulate a limited environment. The current research delves into two types of stochastic perturbation models - one influenced by random fluctuations tied to its existing state, and another combined with an overall level of randomness. The first model, referred to as a metastable stochastic differential equation, typically converges towards equilibrium solutions that remain confined, while the second model results in a type of master equation described as a type of Fokker-Planck equation. The solution to the latter equation decays over a significant period before becoming negligible. The research demonstrates that both types of models exhibit similar behavior over a specific time frame, with the solutions converging towards the same type of equilibrium state. This study provides additional insights into the stability and transformation of stochastic processes that undergo transformation and degradation, with applications extending beyond their initial biological context to a broader field of mathematical and scientific analysis.

The effects of a strong magnetic field on the properties of nuclear matter are examined using the low-energy effective nuclear potential and a modified low-energy universal nuclear potential. The LOCV method is applied to the Schrödinger equation for the lowest possible energy state of symmetric nuclear matter. Our calculations reveal that the lowest energy per nucleon and other properties of nuclear matter are significantly influenced by a magnetic field up to 10^17 Gauss. Furthermore, the results show that the magnetic field's influence on the lowest energy per nucleon varies depending on the type of nuclear potential used.

A key challenge in distributed machine learning involves reconciling the need for secure data with reduced communication costs. To address this, we present an innovative approach that uses homomorphic encryption for privacy and an optimized coding system to lower communication costs while maintaining model accuracy. This method, known as Communication-Efficient Secure Aggregation, can be combined with existing distributed learning methods, such as Federated Averaging, and still offer enhanced security and data protection. Furthermore, we prove that this approach can significantly lower the number of messages exchanged between the server and clients, all while preserving the convergence rate of the model. Experimental results demonstrate that this solution offers better model accuracy and reduced communication costs compared to current federated learning methods, with an additional benefit of secure model delivery.

A comprehensive far-ultraviolet survey of the Taurus-Perseus-Aquila complex revealed significant target selection biases, with a focus on young stars and their circumstellar material. The study successfully obtained high-resolution far-UV observations for 15 young stars within this complex, including three previously unobserved targets. A striking finding was the detection of a strong UV-emitting outflow from the young star TW Hya, which exhibits a velocity of approximately 100 km/s. This is the first time such an outflow has been identified in the far-UV. Additionally, a few other young stars were found to exhibit far-UV emission, which could be attributed to accretion or outflows. A comprehensive catalog of the far-UV data for the complex has been created, which will facilitate future research by providing detailed data on the properties of these young stars.

Table information is often difficult to convey in PDF format due to the limitations of text-based representations. As a consequence, retrieving relevant tables within documents can be an arduous task, even when the associated content is clearly understandable. To address this issue, we introduce GNNs, a novel graph neural network-based representation learning technique, which transforms table structures into interpretable graphs composed of text labels and spatial relationships. The resulting graph-based embeddings are highly effective for table structure representation and content enrichment, significantly enhancing table search capabilities within PDF documents. Our experiments demonstrate that GNNs improve table search recall by 14.6% compared to state-of-the-art graph embedding techniques, and our novel graph construction strategy and embedding methodology offer new avenues for arduous tabular data analysis.

Cognitive hierarchies are commonly used to describe decision-making processes in humans. In this framework, people's reasoning abilities are conceptualized in terms of prediction capabilities, where higher levels of reasoning correspond to knowledge about lower levels and their predictions regarding each other's knowledge. A full reasoner is characterized as one that anticipates all potential predictions. A modified concept of rationality, termed cognitive hierarchy (CH) rationality, posits that each person engages in k rounds of prediction, with the final action choice resulting from kth-order prediction. A distinct form of rationality, called full cognition rationality, involves making an action choice after considering an infinite sequence of prediction levels. A distinct concept, called recursive rationality, suggests that action choice results from reasoning of insufficient depth. To evaluate the effectiveness of CH rationality, we introduce specific solution concepts, including CH rationality in dominant strategies and CH rationality in best responses, and apply them to various game types such as beauty contests, public goods games, and trust games. Our analysis reveals that, in some instances, such as beauty contests, fully rational and recursively rational players converge on equilibrium outcomes, but, in public goods games and trust games, such fully rational and recursively rational players can end up with significantly different outcomes than CH rationality's predictions.

In developing nations, accurate and timely population data is crucial for policy planning. However, gathering this information through traditional censuses proves challenging due to time and resource constraints. As a result, population projections based on older census results in outdated planning decisions. Mozambique, like many developing countries, relies on previous census data for planning purposes because of its large population and difficult terrain, which hinders timely enumeration. To bridge this planning gap, countries like Mozambique need a reliable method for real-time population estimation. The proposed system combines satellite imagery with machine learning to provide autonomous population estimates. By utilizing nighttime lights imagery, the model identifies human settlements and estimates populations, even in areas without visible lights due to power shortages. The project, currently in the early stages, involves collecting and labeling datasets for lighted and unlit areas to improve the model's accuracy.

To address the challenge of the large number of strings encountered in big data applications, researchers have developed a novel collection of data structures called Multi-hashing Polynomial collection (MPP), which efficiently solves the approximate membership query problem. Our proposed structure surpasses existing solutions like the Bloom filter and cuckoo hashing table in both performance and accuracy by providing faster operations and the ability to eliminate potentially malicious inputs that cause excessively high error rates. MPP's polynomial-based design enables it to offer guaranteed false positives only, a property beneficial in various security contexts. Experimental evaluations have shown MPP's superiority over state-of-the-art structures in speed and reliability.

The spin of a dimer is restricted to being composed solely of two spinless fermions, resulting in a restricted, classical-like state despite typically displaying quantum characteristics. We propose an experiment involving recombination of atoms to create an unconventional dimers where the quantum characteristics are amplified by a highly excited state formed through controlled loss, and the quantum nature of this system can be further studied through further interactions induced by a laser pulse.

This study introduces an advanced SPH method that utilizes a multi-resolution approach to enhance the simulation of complex multi-component fluid-structure interactions. This technique leverages a fine mesh to capture crucial details where necessary and a coarser mesh for the overall simulation, thereby optimizing computational efficiency. By integrating this method, researchers can achieve a significant speedup without sacrificing the overall accuracy of the results. Furthermore, this multi-resolution framework enables a more precise modeling of the interface between different phases by strategically placing a high-resolution mesh at the fluid-structure boundary. This method was successfully applied to a series of test cases, encompassing both fluid dynamics and fluid-structure interactions, and was then utilized to study the complex process of cell sedimentation under the influence of a flowing fluid.

A quantum machine learning approach, combining physics-based constraints with machine learning algorithms, is introduced as Quantum Unsupervised and Guided Learning (QUGL). This framework, adaptable to any quantum machine learning algorithm, enhances data representation and parameter initialization. Building on QUGL, a new method is developed that employs constraint-based optimization to enhance the interpretability of classification tasks, allowing for more reliable out-of-distribution data detection. The proposed framework is implemented on superconducting quantum processors and thoroughly evaluated using both synthetic and real-world datasets. Experimental results demonstrate QUGL's effectiveness in improving data representation and parameter initialization, with the classification-based approach enabling more accurate out-of-distribution detection and increased classification accuracy.

A recently developed neural TTS model, FastPitch, has the ability to represent pitch contours while maintaining voice quality comparable to traditional methods. However, a limitation of FastPitch lies in its poor control over pitch when used for tasks like prosody manipulation and expressivity. In this study, a loss function is introduced that enhances pitch controllability without compromising voice quality. It achieves a balance by augmenting pitch values and directly controlling the rate at which pitch values are generated. Notably, the proposed method is simple, lightweight, and efficient. It demonstrates its effectiveness by applying it to FastPitch to accomplish a task, specifically I/O Prosody Manipulation. Experimental findings show that this approach yields improved results in both automatic and subjective evaluations.

This research focuses on addressing the challenge of predicting the dynamic occupancy patterns across spatial locations and diverse hop ranges in spatio-temporal forecasting tasks, such as office space and urban road network predictions. Most existing models, trained on single-hop datasets, struggle to generalize to multi-hop datasets. To address this issue, we introduce Hopper, a transformer-based model capable of making accurate predictions at any hop range with just one training instance. Hopper achieves this adaptability by utilizing a novel, hop-invariant representation learning technique and incorporating an inductive spatial transformer that processes relationships between specific locations within a grid-based input. Furthermore, we enhance the model's performance by employing hop-range adaptive predictive heads, enabling distinct time pattern forecasting for each hop range. Our Hopper model attains superior performance on datasets designed for 75 and 150-hop distances, significantly outperforming leading baselines, and demonstrates robust generalization to 500-hop datasets without requiring retraining.

The Large Hadron Collider's heavy ion experiments have provided valuable data on the large rapidity separation between electrons or muons and $b$-quark pairs, which can be used to understand the properties of the quark-gluon plasma. Researchers have performed the first measurements of this process in proton-proton collisions at the LHC's high-luminosity environment. The study focuses on the creation of leptons and $b\bar{b}$ pairs within a specified momentum range, which is dominated by both vector boson fusion and gluon-fusion processes. The findings are consistent with the Standard Model, and the results can be compared with theoretical calculations from both parton-level and fully integrated data. The study also includes an analysis of the distribution of $W$ bosons' rapidity, which is found to be in agreement with next-to-leading order calculations. The precise measurement of this process is also used to constrain certain parton distribution functions, particularly the flavor-splitting of the bottom-quark.

Assessing the quality of experience (QoE) is a crucial aspect in the development of autonomous systems. In this study, a user-centric approach is introduced for evaluating autonomous vehicle control, which is applied to remote-controlled robots. By utilizing the QoE assessment framework, a study was conducted involving 15 users who completed an interactive visual tracking task with an autonomous robot. The findings indicate that users' satisfaction with the system is influenced by their emotional responses, particularly frustration, as well as their perceived performance. In contrast, cognitive reactions and perceived usability do not show a significant correlation with overall user satisfaction.

This study introduces hierarchical regression models through the integration of Bayesian modeling techniques, beginning with the fundamentals of Bayesian modeling and progressing to the complexities of multi-level data modeling. Our Bayesian approach leverages the Markov chain Monte Carlo method, specifically employing the Gibbs sampler. By demonstrating the construction and application of regression models and the Bayesian analogue, we break down the Bayesian framework into digestible components, including prior specification, likelihood modeling, and posterior analysis. Our multi-level data modeling and Bayesian implementation are then illustrated through a real-world dataset from a study on the influence of coaching on children's baseball batting performance. This work serves as a reference point for those seeking to expand their understanding of Bayesian modeling and its application in the analysis of multi-level data.

This paper offers a novel mathematical interpretation of the Mafia game, providing a well-defined structure that allows us to analyze and understand the rules and gameplay from a mathematical standpoint. By formulating the game in a set-theoretic and combinatorial framework, we are able to derive precise descriptions of Mafia game types, as well as new results within the realms of discrete mathematics, such as properties of specific graphs, matroids, and cellular automata.

Within the solar system, Earth, the most populated planet, is a terrestrial world, whereas Jupiter, the most massive, is a gas giant. The prevailing theory of planet formation suggests that there is a critical point at which a solid planetary core triggers the rapid accumulation of gas, resulting in the formation of a gas giant within a short time frame. However, this process does not explain how Earth avoided accumulating gas from the protoplanetary disk. We have conducted 3D numerical simulations of two planetary embryos interacting with a protoplanetary disk, to study their simultaneous growth and the impact of their mass on the disk's structure. The simulations reveal that significant mass transfer to one embryo can substantially alter the surrounding disk, potentially halting the gas accretion process and allowing it to dissipate, which may account for Earth's avoidance of gas accumulation.

In amorphous-inclusive carbon nanotube films, intertube connections can be hindered by insulating substances, resulting in their low electronic conductivity.
Our study focuses on a novel armchair carbon nanotube film, where phonon-assisted intertube electronic conduction has been demonstrated through phonon current amplification at low temperatures.
This phenomenon was confirmed by observing enhanced phonon-assisted intertube conduction in the carbon nanotube film's resistivity, which also exhibited significantly higher phonon current amplification than its metallic nanotubes counterparts.
Our findings suggest that phonon-assisted intertube conduction plays a significant role in carbon nanotube films even when highly doped, which has significant implications for the understanding of their electronic transport mechanisms and potential applications.

This paper presents a novel clustering approach called EVF-k-Means, which builds on a modified version of the VFK-Means algorithm. Unlike the original VFK-Means, our enhanced algorithm selects data features for weighting based on the Second Law of Thermodynamics, specifically by minimizing total entropy to capture non-linear relationships among features. Our results show that the EVF-k-Means outperforms various benchmarks on both synthetic and real-world datasets, with reduced computational complexity.

Mixture-of-experts models have been utilized in various scenarios, demonstrating the ability to learn complex, non-linear relationships effectively. In a one-dimensional setting, under the assumption of homogeneous experts, researchers discovered that certain aspects of the posterior distribution of such models can't be consistently estimated due to an identification problem. This implies that current Bayesian approaches to training MoE models may be flawed. This work aims to demonstrate two things: Firstly, the generalization performance of Bayesian neural network training using Gibbs sampling is limited, as demonstrated by our results. Secondly, our paper presents an efficient computational method for consistently estimating the 1D homogeneous posterior distribution of a Bayesian linear regression model, which has the computational complexity comparable to that of stochastic gradient descent. This model serves as the simplified version of a mixture-of-experts. The proposed method involves an adaptation of the EM algorithm, which enables consistent estimation of the posterior. The results of our simulation experiments show that this algorithm can outperform Gibbs sampling by an order of magnitude, while also being able to achieve better predictive performance than stochastic gradient descent when using homogeneous mixture-of-experts models.

This investigation delves into chip-firing games conducted on pairs of genus $g$ binary curves, $(C_1, C_2)$, which result in the $M(C_1, C_2)$ matrix and its Davenport-Rosenberg group $G(C_1, C_2)$. The image of $G(C_1, C_2)$ within the Jacobian of the cover, $\mathrm{Jac}(\pi):=J(C_1)\oplus J(C_2)$, is embedded within the Prym variety $P(\pi)$, which in turn is a subvariety of $\mathrm{Jac}(\pi)$. The image under $\mathrm{Jac}(\pi)$ of the identity element of $G(C_1, C_2)$ has dimension $g_1+g_2$, while within $P(\pi)$, this value is $r:=\mathrm{rank}~M(C_1, C_2)$. Consequently, $P(\pi)$'s dimension is $g_1+g_2-r$. Furthermore, the image under $P(\pi)$ of the canonical embedding of $G(C_1, C_2)$ is a subvariety $X$ of a type determined by $r$ and $g_1$, specifically having a genus $2g_1+2g_2-2r$.
