In navigation, map representation plays a crucial role. Existing methods, however, often rely on manually designed representations that may not be optimal. This paper proposes a novel hierarchical topological diagram representation, called HiTMap, inspired by human-built maps, to automatically create optimal navigation maps from sensor data. By combining deep learning and reinforcement learning, HiTMap can segment the environment, represent the grid map hierarchically, and hierarchically plan paths accordingly. The proposed method was tested in simulation with state-of-the-art navigation systems, which favored HiTMap. Furthermore, the paper demonstrates the feasibility of implementing navigation with HiTMap in 2D and 3D domains.

A new class of 2-D binary code sets with low peak side-lobes has been constructed using multivariable functions with controlled differences. These multivariable functions, characterized by their controlled difference properties, allow for the creation of subsets with a difference bound of zero. By leveraging this property, we have developed an inter-group complementary code set and a two-dimensional code set based on Z-supplementary array techniques. The constructed sets exhibit valuable applications in radar systems.

We introduce an innovative variational model to reconstruct polyenergetic CT scans that have been affected by noise. Leveraging the advantages of measuring scan data at various energy levels, where each level provides unique x-ray absorption coefficients, reconstructing the underlying microstructure of an object becomes a non-convex inverse problem. We formulate a probabilistic model, incorporating a non-Gaussian noise sensor, joint with a data fidelity term and a total variation regularization. A non-convex optimization algorithm based on alternating direction of multipliers is proposed, along with a statistical method for estimating the hyperparameters of the model. Through experiments on a synthetic dataset, the proposed model demonstrates its efficacy in CT reconstruction, x-ray absorption coefficient estimation, and x-ray energy binning.

This research investigates how the electron tail and reduced metal work function impact light absorption in subwavelength cavities with nanoscale dielectric spacers. Theoretical calculations show that a metal's electron tail and reduced work function significantly increase the number of gap plasmons supported. Theoretical studies demonstrate that a metal's dielectric constant drops below zero near its work function, indicating a strong interaction between gap plasmons and a metal's electron gas. Theoretical studies show that a metal's electron tail dielectric constant is significantly higher than its local value, indicating a strong nonlocal response. Theoretical studies demonstrate that a metal's electron tail and dielectric constant are highly sensitive to a dielectric spacer's dimensions, indicating that these properties are crucial for understanding the behavior of gap plasmons. The research highlights the importance of considering a metal's electron tail and dielectric constant when designing plasmonic devices, particularly in the limit of vanishing gaps.

In the field of Contextual Named Entity Retrieval, researchers have been working to improve the accuracy of identifying entities based on limited query information. A significant challenge in this area is that traditional methods, which rely on term matching, can be limited by the complexity of names and the presence of irrelevant terms. To address this issue, this paper introduces a context-based scoring approach, Term Relevance Response (TRR), which uses the query context to evaluate the relevance of terms in the document and assigns weights accordingly. By incorporating TRR into Contextual Candidate Access, the proposed framework significantly enhances the performance of context-based name disambiguation and candidate retrieval, resulting in notable improvements in accuracy and precision.

The increasing availability of multivariate time series and longitudinal data has significantly improved our capacity to track and analyze individual growth over time. However, visualizing these complex datasets remains a significant challenge, especially when creating interactive and collaborative experiences. In this study, we address this issue by developing a design framework that facilitates exploration and collaboration on multivariate time series and longitudinal data displayed in various visual formats. By breaking down the multivariate and temporal complexities, we provide a design framework that enables the systematic examination of these issues. Using this framework, we design a range of longitudinal data visualization tools that promote exploration and collaboration, which are then applied to the development of Engage, a new interactive tool for visualizing wearable sensor data. Through a combination of qualitative feedback from data visualization experts and quantitative data from controlled studies, we evaluate the effectiveness of Engage in facilitating exploration and collaboration.

Recent advancements in various fields have been driven by the success of the Graph Neural Network (GNN), which is particularly effective in capturing node embeddings within graphs. However, existing GNN approaches are typically limited to processing homogeneous graphs where node and edge features play the same role. In reality, many applications involve heterogeneous graphs where node features resemble those of edges. A case in point is the analysis of medical records, which can be represented as a graph where individuals and their symptoms are nodes, connected by edges. While traditional GNN methods can analyze these graphs, they fail to exploit the unique characteristics of the nodes. To address this gap, we propose the Heterogeneous Emulation GNN (HERGNN), which incorporates a novel EMulation layer that enables the model to identify node embeddings based on self-resemblance. By integrating heterogeneous node features and designing a novel self-resemblance learning mechanism, HERGNN outperforms existing methods in predicting the medical conditions of individuals.

This study explores the impact of a charged soft polymer's surface polarization on the behavior of an electrolyte solution, using the Poisson-Boltzmann equation to model the system. The surface and ions within the solution are treated as point charges, and the influence of solvent polarization is considered through Kirkwood's theory. A fundamental equation is developed to describe the electric double layer formed on the polymer's surface, and the influence of temperature, solvent properties, and macromolecular chain characteristics on solvent polarization is examined. The study finds that the surface charge density significantly affects solvent polarization, and that the inclusion of surface polarization leads to a more complex and varied system behavior.

This study aims to automatically derive software specifications from organized and implicit document sources. We developed a deep learning-based approach to recognize and translate unstructured text into formatted specifications. Our proposed model integrates a flexible token-basedBNF grammar framework, allowing it to adapt to diverse software specification formats. Evaluation results demonstrate that our approach achieves high accuracy (93.2%) in generating correct syntax for small software specifications and 96.0% precision and recall for document element extraction.

A one-way communication network is analyzed with a focus on energy efficiency, incorporating network coding at the intermediate nodes. To optimize energy consumption in this network, we've developed an innovative scheduling approach combined with power allocation that yields a convex problem, which can be solved efficiently. Our energy allocation method, utilizing energy allocation fraction variables, reduces computational complexity. Comparative results with other schemes demonstrate the proposed model's superior performance.

A theoretical framework combining the Dirac equation with the non-collinear and non-collineation of magnetism has been applied to a specific surface system, specifically an manganese atom and manganese clusters that have been placed on the (110) surface of niobium. The research examined the development of specific states in this system, known as Yu--Shiba--Rusinov states, by leveraging a specific approximation to simplify the quantum mechanical calculations. The results of this study provided accurate predictions regarding the observed properties of these states in existing experimental studies, and also explored how these states evolve in terms of energy, position, and characteristics as the number of manganese atoms in the clusters increased. The research's findings are expected to contribute to the development of more accurate and computationally efficient methods for modeling this specific class of magnetic impurities on superconducting surfaces.

This paper introduces an approach to address the issue of scale invariant distribution matching that suffers from bias due to the use of Euclidean distance, which we refer to as bias-aware D2D match. We propose a method that involves normalizing the feature vector distributions through a two-step process to create a bias-reduced scoring function based on Earth Mover's Distance. Furthermore, we develop a deep learning based algorithm to efficiently approximate this score function and present experimental results demonstrating its effectiveness, which surpasses state-of-the-art methods in both accuracy and efficiency.

Satellite imagery analysis has traditionally relied on computer vision techniques, but deep learning has recently become the go-to method due to its high performance and ease of use. Despite its success, deep learning's requirement for large, high-quality datasets and the lack of interpretability pose significant challenges. This research aims to address these issues by showcasing the benefits of a hand-crafted, rule-based approach designed to simulate human-like vision, particularly in identifying object boundaries within satellite photos. By utilizing a combination of color, texture, and shape cues, this system demonstrates impressive edge detection capabilities comparable to, and in some cases, superior to, state-of-the-art deep learning models. Moreover, it offers greater efficiency and adaptability, making it a promising alternative to deep learning in various satellite photo analysis tasks.

Traditional techniques for studying the valence electron configurations of atoms, such as X-ray absorption spectroscopy, have been limited by the assumption of linear spectral signals. However, recent experiments have demonstrated non-linear X-ray spectra at high fluence, rendering these traditional methods ineffective. These findings are attributed to the presence of specific excited states, such as double core excitations, which occur at elevated fluence levels. To better capture these non-linear signals, we introduce a novel model grounded in the rate theory of double core excitations. This model enables the integration of both single- and double-core excitations, yielding an enhanced understanding of the valence electron configurations, even at non-linear spectral fluence levels. Our research showcases the model's efficacy in analyzing data obtained from a time-resolved pump-probe experiment, where it was employed to investigate the dynamics of a closed 3d shell in transition metals. Furthermore, we demonstrate that a comprehensive model is essential for accurately interpreting such non-linear spectral signals.

Research into the reliability of Machine Learning (ML) models has led to the development of adversarial attacks and defenses as methods for testing and improving model resilience. However, little work has been done on the application of these concepts in Modulation Classification (MC) within Software Defined Radio (SDR). This research aims to fill this void by introducing MCSAD, a novel method of ad-versarial training specifically designed to enhance the robustness of MC models against various types of adversarial attacks. Our approach, based on a conditional generation model, is effective across diverse scenarios, including attacks aimed at specific or general classifiers and challenges imposed by signal distortions and impairments. Additionally, we evaluate the potential threats of a dual-risk scenario in which a malicious actor intentionally trains a classifier to exploit a pre-trained robust model. Results demonstrate that our method surpasses conventional MC techniques in adversarial training and rivals State-of-the-Art (SOTA) models under severe attacks.

Continuing to learn from where a model currently stands, rather than starting from scratch, is often the best approach when adapting to new, related problems. However, the scientific community has yet to rigorously demonstrate this concept. To explore this idea, a study examined the use of a cutting-edge, memory-based 3D neural network called MCAU3D in diagnosing a complex disease, Multiple Sclerosis, across different hospitals' scans. The results showed that continuous learning from where a model currently stands, even with its existing weaknesses, is more effective than training from scratch when the goal is to improve diagnostic accuracy on new data while maintaining performance on existing data.

A novel technique known as Bipolar Contrast has been developed to generate bipolar images with positive and negative features, transforming the traditional imaging process. This innovative approach, unlike the established monopolar comparison method, enables the creation of a more compact and higher-order bipolar signal. In addition, a novel image coding framework has been proposed, allowing for the creation of a bipolar image from a bipolar signal and a bipolar codebook. This framework offers the possibility of developing a range of image coding schemes, each with their own advantages. Experiments conducted on the LUng CT dataset demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach by achieving better compression and visual quality than the state-of-the-art LUCA monopolar compression. Specifically, the best results show a 10% reduction in bitrate and an increase in bipolar CS-PSNR by 0.16dB compared to LUCA.

A key goal in data-driven control is to develop a precise model from the given data. However, the inherent uncertainty in the data can lead to models filled with noise and errors. This paper introduces a data-driven approach to a key issue in control theory - identifying models with significant mistakes or inaccuracies. Unlike previous methods, our technique does not assume a specific structure for the model or its error, allowing for both deterministic and stochastic error analysis. By breaking down these errors into measurable quantities, our method enables the identification of models that have made substantial mistakes. A simulation example is presented to demonstrate the method's effectiveness in handling both structured and unstructured errors.

A well-known star-forming region, the Dragon IRCQ, exhibits a distinct core structure, 
characterized by a core-to-envelope mass ratio of 80%, indicating an advanced stage of contraction.
This paper explores the complex interplay between the region's core and its surrounding envelope, 
revealing the presence of a core expansion phenomenon. The expansion velocity of the core, 
measured at 0.56 km/s, is significantly higher than the speed of sound, 0.25 km/s, 
indicating that the core is not in a state of hydrostatic equilibrium. The data also reveal 
evidence of a core expansion velocity increase over the course of 1.1 years, 
indicative of a core expansion triggered by an external force. The magnitude of the core's 
expansion is comparable to that of other massive star-forming regions, 
indicative of the potential for the Dragon IRCQ to form a massive star in the future.

This paper introduces PopSyCLE, a Python framework for the post-processing of Primordial Black Hole formation, initially built upon the C++ program PSFVC++. Primordial Black Holes, which may have formed during the dark ages of Primordial Fluids, are a potential candidate for dark matter, with their mass believed to be in the $10^{-16}-10^{-2}$ solar mass range. To better understand the relationship between PBH formation and dark matter, this paper provides the first calculations using PopSyCLE. With Primordial Black Holes remaining unconfirmed, population studies of PBHs are crucial, with PopSyCLE contributing to the understanding of gravitational wave signals from PBH mergers detectable by LIGO and Virgo.

This study examines a system of uniformly sized spherical wedge molecules consisting of spheres of fixed radius. Through Monte Carlo simulations, we analyzed the behavior of this system in two and three dimensions. Our research identified distinct liquid, solid, and solid-like phases characterized as a kinked liquid (KL), a playhouse solid (PS), and a twisted solid (TS), respectively. These phases exhibit unique ordering patterns, such as the formation of disclinations in the solid's orientation order and localized regions of orientational disorder. The findings are consistent with those of a triangular wedge system, while displaying distinct properties. Notably, the melting transitions of the system were found to be continuous in two dimensions and first-order in three dimensions.

Adjusting pre-trained models for various downstream tasks often requires significant
parameter modifications, which can be computationally expensive and time-consuming.
To alleviate this issue, we propose a novel method called ST-Adapter that utilizes a
special token to represent task-specific information and incorporates it into the
model's existing structure. By doing so, it enables efficient adaptation of the model
with a minimal set of parameters. We conducted experiments on multiple benchmark
datasets and found that ST-Adapter outperforms other Adapter-based approaches in
terms of accuracy and efficiency, particularly in complex tasks such as multi-task
learning and low-resource adaptation.

This study explores the application of preference information in addressing optimization issues under subjective preferences and uncertainty, where an a priori preference relation among criteria value profiles guides the decision-maker. We examine the impact of incorporating preference information on a set of criteria outcomes, acknowledging that fully capturing a decision-maker's preference structure is often impractical, leading to the consideration of partial preference information on subsets of outcomes. Our focus is on the efficiency of using partial preference information versus global but context-dependent preference information, highlighting the rich structure of contextual preference notions and their connections to Skorsky's decomposition of value functions.

A general theory for polymers in the liquid state suggests that specific thermodynamic properties, such as the glass transition temperature and coefficients, are directly related to certain dynamic properties, including relaxation times and activation energies. This theory is examined through data comparison and evidence suggests that some of these relationships accurately hold, yet others show significant deviations, indicating a more complex scenario. Notably, discrepancies arise in the temperature dependency of cooperative relaxation, suggesting that scaling laws, such as the Vogel-Fulcher-Tammhaus equation, become invalid near the glass transition temperature. Consequently, a simplified theoretical model, assuming a single temperature for activation energy, may not be sufficient to describe the liquid state of glass-forming polymers and further research is required to develop a comprehensive solution.

Text generation models like transformer-based language models are becoming increasingly capable, yet they are still susceptible to producing text that lacks realism and coherence. The current study investigates how rejecting inappropriate tokens during the generation process can be integrated into a transformer model through the analysis of attention patterns. By analyzing the function of negative attention, the research demonstrates that suppressing the primary attention head in a multi-head attention model enhances token selection by reducing over-reliance on key phrases. As a result, the modified model exhibits greater diversity in its text output. Furthermore, the research explores the relationship between attention patterns and token relevance. Ultimately, the study contributes to the understanding of rejecting token choices in text generation by using the model's inherent properties to inform subsequent design decisions.

In the context of neural machine translation, our approach focuses on improving the lookahead mechanism, particularly how it is utilized during generation. Our analysis reveals that most existing lookahead strategies are limited in scope, often focusing on specific aspects of the target sequence, such as its beginning or end. In contrast, we suggest that generation processes should instead concentrate on the most likely location of new output being generated at any given time. To address this issue, we propose the Lookahead Focus of Mass Entropy (LFOME) strategy, which utilizes an enhanced version of the Dirichlet distribution to estimate the probability distribution of where the next output will be generated. Our experimental findings demonstrate the superiority of LFOME over other lookahead strategies in terms of performance and efficiency.

This study calculates the Kontsevich weights for graphs representing connections and curvature curvature effects within symplectic-poisson geometry, also known as 'universal symplectic gravity theories'. These calculations are then used to formulate universal symplectic gravity theories at the levels of connection and curvature, which are subsequently applied to compute the symplectic gravity expansion of the classical action for a general symplectomorphism near a constant symplectomorphism.

A method has been developed to analyze the thermal state of large $N$ CFTs with a wide range of couplings, by determining a key parameter $\mu$ that controls the behavior of the theory. This analysis reveals that the effective dual geometry transitions from an anti-de Sitter space to a black hole space when $\mu$ exceeds a specific threshold. In the regime where $\mu$ is below this threshold, the mutual information between the thermal state and the vacuum grows exponentially with the dimension of the large $N$ limit, while in the opposite regime, the theory becomes disconnected from the vacuum, exhibiting a property known as "area law" behavior. This analysis also reveals a new mechanism for "area law" behavior, which is distinct from previously observed phenomena. Furthermore, the analysis has uncovered a new phase transition, which is distinct from previously known transitions, and has provided insights into the behavior of the effective dual geometry at large $N$ limits.

The method presented in the given paper utilizes an approximation technique, enabling it to transform any Asian option pricing problem into a series of options on a Markov process. This result in a significant decrease in computational time when employing finite difference methods for pricing. The method's effectiveness is demonstrated through the application of a hybrid finite element/finite volume method, the spectral method for spatial diffusion, and the finite volume method for highly oscillatory test functions, ultimately producing swift and reliable pricing algorithms for double Asian put options.

Gamma-ray observations of individual galaxy clusters have posed a significant challenge to current models, yet the combined gamma-ray flux from all galaxy clusters is largely unexplained.  We hypothesize that the missing signal originates from galaxy clusters with lower energies below the Field of View of Fermi-LAT.  By utilizing the differential cluster count data from the XMM-Cluster Survey, we developed models to predict gamma-ray emissions from sub-threshold galaxy clusters and combined them with the observed higher-energy flux from the Fermi-LAT. The foundational "features" in theoretical models of inflationary features, such as features, cosmic strings, or black holes, can potentially produce the cosmological collider signal. Using mathematical calculations based on the perturbation theory of conformal interaction, researchers have examined the single-mode or 2-to-1 correlation functions, which produce cosmological fingerprints. These studies have also assessed the conditions under which these features, characterized by their non-Bunch-Davies states, can produce observable cosmological collider signals. Furthermore, researchers have explored the conditions under which primordial power spectra can produce cosmological collider signals in theories featuring feature-driven inflation.

This study aims to enhance the interpretability of pre-trained deep convolutional neural networks by targeting their inner workings, specifically intermediate features and kernels. A proposed approach, called as ConvNetExplainer, leverages non-negative matrix factorization to simultaneously analyze features and kernels, mapping visual patterns in the network's intermediate layers to the activation of the most influential higher-level filters that connect to the final classification layer. ConvNetExplainer's analysis is further validated through the examination of its correspondence with semantic word embeddings, utilizing both GloVe and Word2Vec models. The results show that as features are activated in the network, they progress from low-level details to higher-level concepts, culminating in the final classification.

A one-dimensional electronic system inherently tends to fragment over a broad spectrum of parameters into small segments isolated from each other by energy barriers that prevent conductive connections. Our research demonstrates that these repulsive barriers can be overcome and attractive connections between segments can occur, specifically, by considering a single band in the cuprate materials, where the attractive connections occur, specifically, at the edges of the momentum spectrum. The attractive connections occur, specifically, due to phonon-mediated mechanisms, which involve a combination of electron-phonon repulsion and the attraction caused when two electrons exchange a phonon, which reduces the total energy when the particles are further apart, and overcomes the repulsive electron-phonon forces at the edges of the momentum spectrum, and results in bonding states, which bind the segments together, and results in a significant increase in energy, and results in a significant decrease in the probability of finding electrons apart from each other, and results in a significant decrease in the probability of finding segments together, and results in a significant decrease in the probability of segments bonding together, and results in a significant decrease in the probability of segments bonding together, and results in a significant decrease in the probability of segments bonding together, and results in a significant decrease in the probability of segments bonding together.

A novel individual-level Indian IHIS dataset is available for causal structure learning, but a challenge arises due to its lack of complete family history information, which is essential for learning causal structures across generations. To overcome this limitation, a new approach is proposed that utilizes a detailed dataset of 1,000 subjects, which is complemented by simulations demonstrating the efficacy of the proposed method in generating accurate family histories and learning causal structures across generations. The results show that by fusing prior knowledge and data, a more complete understanding of multi-generational causal structures can be achieved.

The existence of unstable topological textures, such as Majorana zero modes and Majorana fermions, holds significant interest for topological quantum computing. We discovered a unique unstable skyrmion phase in the magnetic compound Co$_9$Zn$_9$Mn$_2$, which featured a complete phase diagram dependent on temperature and magnetic field strength. As the magnetic field increased, the sample exhibited a complex behavior, transitioning from a conventional paramagnetic phase directly into a stable C10 skyrmion phase, and then to an unstable C10 phase with topological properties, before finally entering a cone phase. Furthermore, the cone phase demonstrated a complex transition into two distinct phases, which could be a stripe phase separated from an unstable C10 phase, and a stripe phase separated from another competing cone phase with topological properties. To study these unique phases, we employed $\mu_0$H = 2 T and performed experiments using muon spin relaxation and muon relaxation and resonance, which revealed that the unstable skyrmion phase exhibited a unique characteristic with a frequency that varied as $\mu_0$H$^{-0.58}$ and exhibited a complex temperature dependence that was distinct from other phases. We found that the unstable skyrmion phase exhibited a frequency that varied as $\mu_0$H$^{-0.58}$ and that this variation was distinct from other phases. This article provides a comprehensive overview of high-dimensional variable selection techniques, particularly within dynamic linear models, and examines the current literature on the topic. These variable selection approaches have become increasingly popular in the field of statistics, yet dynamic models have received relatively less attention. The article begins by introducing variable selection for static linear regression and then explores its application to dynamic models, reviewing recent variable selection methods and discussing their relevance to dynamic settings. Finally, it identifies areas for future research and highlights the limitations of existing variable selection techniques when applied to dynamic models.

This paper introduces a straightforward and user-friendly algorithm to solve the equilibrium problem, demonstrating its convergence under plausible assumptions. We also apply a iterative method based on the equilibrium problem to resolve a convex optimization problem and the split monotone variational inequality problem, achieving a new convergent solution. Furthermore, conditions for the convergence in probability of the proposed algorithm are established.

A recently developed technique for data hiding in deep neural networks has been criticized for its reliance on a fixed, non-adaptive hiding pattern. In response, an improved, operator-based technique has been proposed, which allows the hiding pattern to be generated dynamically based on channel conditions. However, this novel approach requires a two-way communication channel, which may not be available in all scenarios. To address this limitation, we propose a new form of reversible hiding technique that builds on the improvements of operator-based methods while still utilizing the sender's available channel information in a one-way communication setup. Furthermore, our experimental results demonstrate that operator-based concealment and the traditional statistic-based approach are both outperformed by our proposed reversible hiding technique.

A mean-field approach is used to study how convective turbulence impacts global dynamos, particularly axially symmetric ones, in spherical environments. An empirical model for turbulent magnetic field effects is developed, incorporating previous findings on turbulence and the effects of magnetic fields, and then applied to a simplified dynamo model. The effect of turbulent pumping is found to be more significant in the convection envelope of K2V stars and the Sun compared to outer convective regions of A-F type main sequence stars. To accurately capture the dynamics of convective turbulence, the full spectrum of turbulent effects must be considered.

The galaxy NGC4945, a Seyfert 2, displays signs of a molecular ejecta due to the effects of a powerful ionizing source. The galaxy's supermassive black hole is thought to be responsible for this phenomenon, with the effects of a powerful wind pushing gas away from the center. The ALMA telescope has detected carbon monoxide emissions from the ejecta, revealing that the gas is moving at high speeds. The temperature of the gas is estimated to be around 100 Kelvin, and the gas is being compressed by the galaxy's dense interstellar medium. The ALMA telescope's data also suggests that the gas is being affected by the galaxy's dense interstellar medium, with the gas's properties changing as it moves away from the galaxy's center. The results of this research provide new insights into the complex interplay between black hole winds and the galaxy's interstellar medium.

A sophisticated numerical algorithm has been developed to solve complex magnetized plasma problems, encompassing problems with and without certain types of magnetic characteristics. This approach relies on a specialized finite element method tailored to particular boundary conditions and utilizes a specialized numerical integration technique capable of precisely handling both types of magnetized problems while maintaining a level that exactly conserves key physical quantities. The algorithm's performance has been thoroughly evaluated through the use of classic benchmark tests, confirming its ability to precisely model various phenomena, including the intricate dynamics of magnetic field interactions and the behavior of particles in magnetic fields.

A class of differential equations has been studied, with stepsize variable SDIMSIMs developed to solve an initial value problem. By deriving an exponential trapezoidal method and proving that it achieves the expected order of convergence, a BDF-SDIMSIM composite method is created. It is then demonstrated that this composite method reaches the expected order of convergence for an arbitrary stepsize, reaching the expected order of convergence when the stepsize tends to zero. Lastly, the efficiency of the approach is confirmed by running tests.

We propose a method to prove the exponential stability of a C0-semigroup generated by an infinitesimal generator A, using a Lyapunov equation C0-semigroup equation, particularly focusing on infinite-dimensional Hilbert spaces where rank-infinite C semium matrices are employed. Given a self-adjoint C-infinite matrix C≥0 and a generator matrix A, the Lyapunov equation AX+XC' = X'C' = CX = -Q≤0, where Q is also a self-adjoint matrix, enables us to establish stability conditions through its solution. Furthermore, under specific conditions, including equivalence of C and the identity matrix in the weak topology, the norm equivalence leads to the comparison of the generated C0-semigroups and the spectral radius of the inverse matrix C-1/2AC-1/2, allowing us to establish a relationship between the solution to the Lyapunov equation and the exponential stability of the generated C0-semigroup.

The muon pair collider, a proposed next-generation machine, is anticipated to significantly contribute to fundamental physics research. Two new particles, the muonium and dimuonium atoms, are among many potential discovery targets at this collider. To facilitate experimental research, a novel calculator called MuMuPy has been developed to support the investigation of the interaction between muon pair atoms and external substances, including their scattering and absorption processes, and the measurement of various cross-sections. This calculator is open-source and available for download from GitHub under the (Apache-2.0) license, and can be accessed at the following link: https://github.com/ICHEC-HEP/MuMuPy.

Portfolio managers often assess performance through dual metrics: individual portfolio returns relative to market trends, all while considering total asset value. To address this assessment method, investors' risk preferences can be represented using a power utility function that depends on both the absolute and relative asset levels, resulting in a new optimization framework. We convert this into an Merton-type problem and derive closed-form solutions for constant or step-wise interest rates, demonstrating that our approach effectively unifies existing models such as Sharpe ratio maximization with absolute or relative returns. Furthermore, our results align with those of the Black-Scholes strategy for risk-free borrowing and repayment. When the interest rate is positive, our strategy differs from the standard Merton strategy in terms of weights, variance, and allocation. Conversely, a decrease in the interest rate leads to increased allocation in risky assets, a phenomenon known as the wealth effect.

The cosmic evolution of dwarf galaxies is heavily influenced by the surrounding intergalactic medium, specifically its thermal and ionization conditions. The IGM, in turn, undergoes its own changes as a result of gas accretion onto dwarf galaxies. The IGM's properties are a result of complex interactions between gravitational forces and feedback from the galaxies. The IGM's state can be studied through observations of hydrogen emission and absorption, as well as the cooling rates of hydrogen and molecular ions. The thermal and chemical properties of the IGM can be determined by analyzing these observations, providing valuable insights into the evolution of the galaxies and the surrounding environment.

We examine the thermal conductivity and specific heat of a model that comprises itinerant fermions and local bosons interacting with each other, and find that, contrary to previous studies, the thermal conductivity does not decrease to zero as the coupling strength increases, but instead exhibits a peak. This unusual phenomenon is caused by the local bosons forming correlations with the fermions, which significantly suppresses their movement. Importantly, the local bosons themselves do not contribute to the thermal conductivity, and this behavior occurs in a region where there is no metallic-like peak in the thermal conductivity, and also at a point where the specific heat reaches a minimum. This phenomenon occurs at and around a point where the thermal conductivity reaches its maximum, and also at and around a point where the specific heat reaches its minimum, which is away from a point where the thermal conductivity reaches its minimum, and also at and around a point where the specific heat reaches its maximum. This behavior occurs in a region where there is no metallic-like peak, and also at a point where the specific heat reaches its minimum.

The divergence function, which measures how quickly the distance from a reference point grows, can be considered an indicator of a group's geometry. This paper examines the divergence functions of several notable groups including the pure and fundamental braided Thompson groups, as well as the braided Thompson group V, and determines that they exhibit a type of divergence referred to as "type p" for any finite positive p. In contrast, the divergence functions of the various Thompson groups and their counterparts, such as V_, V+, and V0, are found to exhibit infinite growth. Furthermore, this study reveals that the divergence functions of the pure braid groups, the fundamental braided Thompson groups, and the thread Thompson group F all have a type of divergence that can be arbitrarily chosen as a positive real number p.

This article examines the possibility of adapting the Dual Encoder DPR retriever, a key component in the RAG framework, for a specific domain, such as medical questions. Specifically, we explore the effectiveness of a relatively underutilized approach, where a dual encoder model is treated as a standalone classifier and adapted for a specific domain, as opposed to continuing pre-training with the general corpus. We also investigate the impact of a domain-specific dataset of medical questions, including various training methods, such as multi-task learning, in achieving accurate responses. Through systematic experimentation, we demonstrate the feasibility of this specific domain adaptation approach and identify the most effective methods for achieving high performance. Our findings provide valuable insights for researchers working on the RAG framework and the adaptation of NLP models to specific domains, such as medicine.

This study derives a simple and direct proof of the asymptotic behavior of polynomials that are orthogonal with respect to a log-weighted measure, where the weight is defined by $w(x,\rho,\epsilon):=(x^\epsilon-1)^{\rho}\exp(-\frac{1}{\epsilon}(x^\epsilon-1))$ on the interval $(0,1)$, involving real parameters $\epsilon\in(0,1)$, $\rho>0$, and provides a solution that applies uniformly across this parameter space, while also extending to $\epsilon=0$ and revealing new insights into the asymptotic behavior of the corresponding Jacobi polynomials when $\rho$ approaches 0.

A multitude of studies rely on crowdsourcing, yet their dependencies on the quality of crowd workers' responses are often overlooked. A lack of effective screening methods forces researchers to either trust crowd workers or discard large amounts of data in the search for suitable workers. This study aims to create innovative approaches to automatically identify and screen competent crowd workers. Our research reveals that existing screening methods are inadequate and highly inaccurate. In an effort to improve worker screening, we put forth the following key contributions: (1) an investigation into the current state of crowd worker screening and its significant shortcomings; (2) novel ideas and techniques for developing more precise screening tools; (3) the creation of diverse, large-scale datasets designed to facilitate the creation of robust screening tools; (4) the development of specific tools to manage and maintain a crowd worker database; (5) the design of a crowdsourcing platform, 'CrowdKeep,' that incorporates advanced screening tools; and (6) the performance evaluation of proposed screening tools using the CrowdKeep system and database. Our research indicates that our new screening methods can significantly reduce data collection costs, with up to 80% fewer responses needed to achieve the same level of accuracy.

Text-text image search has been a long-standing challenge in the field, with recent advances in visual question answering and image captioning driving renewed interest. Current approaches often rely on the assumption that descriptions and text images are unrelated, leading to difficulties in linking descriptions to their visual counterparts. To address these limitations, a novel approach called TS2-Net is proposed, which incorporates a transformer-based model that incorporates motion information and selects the most relevant description features. By doing so, TS2-Net achieves state-of-the-art results with its capability to effectively integrate description features and improve overall performance.

A new flavor-changing neutral current process, specifically $t\bar{t}g\gamma$, is investigated in the context of a hypothetical non-standard model that includes flavor-changing $gg \to t\bar{t}$ and $\gamma g \to t\bar{t}$ interactions. This model is characterized by the presence of a single non-standard coupling constant, which is denoted as $C_8^{t\bar{t}}$. In the event of CP violation, a complex phase is associated with this interaction. A detailed analysis of the production cross-section for the $t\bar{j}g\gamma$ process, where j represents a jet, is conducted within the context of the Standard Model and a variety of non-standard models. These models incorporate both a $C_8^{q\bar{q}}$ interaction and a $C_8^{q\bar{q}\prime}$ interaction. A method for determining the magnitude and phase of the non-standard interactions is developed, utilizing $\mathrm{t\bar{t}}$ events with jet multiplicity of 2, 3, and 4 in the associated production of top quarks. Additionally, the production of a single top quark is examined in the context of the non-standard model, where interactions of type $t\bar{q}g$ and $t\bar{q}\gamma$ are present.
